The Winnebago tent nsed for sacred dances is long and narrow ; not more\nthan 20 feet wide and varying from 50 to 100 feet long.\n\nIn the Buffalo dance, which is given four times in the month of May and early\nJune, the dancers are four men and a large number of women. As the dancers enter\neach woman brings in a handful of tine earth and in this way two mounds are raised\nin the center at the east — that is, between the eastern entrance and the fire, which\nis abont 15 feet from the eastern entrance. The mounds thus formed are truncated\ncones. An old man said to me, \"That is the way all mounds were built; that is\nwhy we build so for the buffalo.\"\n\nThe mounds were about 4 inches high and not far from 18 inches in diameter. On\ntop of the mounds were placed the head-gear worn by the men, the claws, tails, and\nother articles used by the four leaders or male dancers.\n\nThe men imitate the buffalo in his wild tramping and roaring, and dance with\ngreat vigor. They are followed by a long line of gaily decked women in single file.\nEach woman as she dances keeps her feet nearly straight and heels close together,\nand the body is propelled forward by a series of jerks which Jars the whole frame,\nbut the general effect on the long, closely packed line is that of the undulating\nappearance of a vast herd moving.\n\n> Mis8 Fletcher iu Am. Assoc. Adv. Sci., Proo. Mluoeapolis meeting, 1883. Salem, 1884. pp. 396, 897.\n\nThe women dance with their eyes turned toward the ground and with their hands\nhanging closely in front, palms next to the person. The track left by their feet is\nvery pretty, being like a close-leaved vine. It is astonishing to notice how each\nwoman can leap into her predecessor's track. Water is partaken of and the entire\ndance is clearly indicative of the prayer for increase and plenty of buffalo. The\ntwo mounds remind one of larger structures and suggest many speculations, particularly when taken in connection with the manner of their building.\n\nIn the g^eat mystery lodge, whence so many of the sacred societies among other\ntribes professedly take their rise and inspiration, the fire is at the east, and is made\nby placing four sticks meeting in the center and the other ends pointing to the four\npoints of the compass.' Just at that part of the initiation of the candidate when\nhe is to fall dead to the old life, be covered as with a pall, and then be raised to the\nnew life, the remains of the four sticks are taken away and the ashes raised in a\nsharp conical mound, again suggesting hints of a peculiar past.\n\nUpon the bluffs'of the Missouri, on a promontory * '^ * is a little depression\ncutiu the ground, circular in form, with an elongated end at the east. The depression\nis 1 foot in diameter and about 6 inches deep. Placing my compass in the center,\nthe long end or entrance was found to be exactly to the east. To the south of this\nsacred spot, for it is cleared and cleanea * « * every year, stood a large cedar\ntree, now partly blown down. This was the sacred tree on which miraculous impersonation of visions lit ; and here the spirits tarried as they passed fh>m one resting\nplace to another going over the country. About every 50 miles there is one of these\nstrange, supernatural resting places."
}

quoted in this study as stating the Dakota belief in a Great Spirit,

efficacy.

The same writer records that "Wahconda" appeared sometimes as
a grizzly bear, sometimes as a bison, at others as a beaver, or an owl,
or some other bird or animal.^ It is plain that Say mistook the generic
term, '* Wahconda," for a specitic one. (See §§ 6, 21-24.)

Shea says :

Although polytheism did not exist, although they all recognized one Supreme
Being, the creator of all, • * • they nowhere adored the God whom they knew.
* * * The demons with which they peopled nature, these alone, in their fear they
sought to appease. * * * Pure unmixed devil-worship prevailed throughout the
length and breadth of the land.^

§ 93. Lynd made some very pertinent remarks:

A stranger coming among the Dakotas for the first time, and observing the endless
variety of objects upon which they bestow their devotion, and the manifold forms
which that worship assumes, at once pronounces them pantheists. A further acquaintance with them convinces him that they are pantheists of no ordinary kind —

at the name — one makes a religion of the raw fish feast, while another stands by and
laughs at his performance — and others, listening to the supposed revelations of the

§ 106. In the worship of their deities x)aint forms an important feature.
Stjarlet or red is the religious color for sacrifices, while blue is used by
the women in many of the ceremonies in which they participate (§§ 374,
376). This, however, is not a constant distinction of sex, for the women
frequently use red or scarlet. Tlie use of i)aints the Dakotas aver was
taught tliem by the gods.^

For accounts of the Sun-dance and a sacrifice to the Dawn, see §§ 141,
21 1, 215.

THE UNKTEHI, OR SUBAQtTATIO AND SUBTERRANEAN POWERS.

§ 106. The gods of this name, for there are many, are the most powerfiil
of all. In their external form they are said to resemble the ox, only
they are of immense i)roportions. They can extend their horns and
tails 80 as to reach the skies. These are the organs of their i)ower.
According to one account the Unktelii inhabit all deep waters, and
especially all great waterfalls. Two hundied and eleven years ago,
wheh Hennepin and Du Luth saw the Falls of St. Anthony together,
there were some buffalo robes hanging there as sacrifices to the UnkteUi
of the ])lace.*

§107. Another account written by the same author informs us that
the male Unktelii dwell in the water, and the spirits of the females
animate the earth. Hence, when the Dakota seems to be offering
sacrifices to the water or the earth, it is to this family of gods that the
worship is rendered. They address the males as ^'grandfathers," and
the females as " grandmotjiers." It is believed that one of these gods

  "passage_text": "THE AEMOR GODS.\n\n§ 122. As each young man comes to maturity a tutelar divinity, sometimes called ''Wa.4icui)\" (see §236), is .assigned to him. It is the spirit of some\nbird or animal, as the wolf, beaver, loon, or eagle. He must not kill\ntliis auiinal, but hold it ever sacred, or at least until he has proved his\nmanhood by killing an enemy. Frequently the young man forms an\nimage of this saxn ed animal and carries it about with him, regarding\nit as having a direct infiuence upon his everyday life and ultimate\ndestiny. Parkman says (in his ''Jesuits in North America,'' p. lxxi,\n\n' Poml, Minn. UiHt. Soc. Coll., vol. ii, pt. 3, p. 43. Riggs, Tab-koo Wabkon, pp. 62-64.\n\n'MisrtiouH and MiaHinnarion. p. 143.\n\n■Smet. op. cit.. p. i:M.\n\n* Maximiliaii, Travels iu Nortb America, p. 107.\n\nV.\n\n444 A bTUDY OF SIOUAN CULTS.\n\nnote) that the knowledge of this guardian spirit comes through dreams\nat the initiatory fast. If this is ever true among the Dakota, it is not\nthe rule. This knowledge is communicated by the \" war prophet.\" ^\n(See §§120, 127, 129, 305, etc.)\n\nAshley tells us that among the Sisseton and Wahpeton Dakota the\nwarrior, as such, wa^s forbidden by custom of law to eat the tongue,\nhead, or heart of many beasts. There were other animals of which the\nheads might be eaten, but not the tongues. A warrior about to go on\nthe war path could not have intercourse with women, but must go\nthrough the purification of the inipi or sweat bath, which lasts four\ndays. A married warrior could not touch his own weapons until he\nhad thus purified himself.*\n\n§ 123. The Armor god and the Spirit of the mystery sack are sometimes spoken of as if they were individual and separate divinities ; but\nthey seem rather to be the god-power which is put into the armor and\nsack by consecration. They should be regarded as the indwelling of\nthe Unktehi or of the TakuskanSkan. A young man's war weapons\nare wakan and must not be touched by a woman. A man prays to his\narmor in the day of battle. In the consecration of these weapons of\nwar and the hunt a young man comes under certain taboo restrictions.\nCertain parts of an animal are sacred and must not be eaten until he\nhas killed an enemy. ^"

From him he also receiveii those paints\nwhich serve as an armature for the body. To obtain these necessaiy\narticles the proud applicant is required for a time to abuse himself and\nsei've him, while he goes through a series of painful and exhausting\nperformances which are necessary on his part to enlist the favorable\nnotice ot the gods. These performances consist chiefly of vapor baths,\nfastings, chants, prayers, and nightly vigils. The spear and the tomahawk being prepared and consecrated, the person who is to receive\nthem approaches the wakan man and presents a pii)e to him. He a^ks\na favor, in substance as follows : *' Pity thou me, poor and helpless, a\nwoman, Jind confer on me the ability to perform manly deeds.^ The\nprophet gives him the weapons and tells him not to forget liis vows to\nthe gods when he returns iu triumph, a man. The weapons are carefully preserved by the warrior. They are wrapped in cloth, together\n\n1 RiggR. Tab koo Wah-kou, pp, 69, 70.\n\n>K«v. K. In fair weather they are hiid outside of the\nlodge every day. They must never be touched by an adult female. *\n\n§ 125. Lynd's account is slightly diflferent, though insubstantial accord\nwith the preceding one :\n\nWhen a youth nrrives at the age proper for going on the warpath ho first purifies\nhimself by fasting and the inipi or steam bath for throe days, and then goes, with\ntears in his eyes, to some wakan man whose influence is undoubted, and prays that\nhe win present him with the wotawe or consecrated armor. This wakan man is\nusuany some old and experienced zuya wakan or sacred war leader. Aftor a time\nthe armor is presented to the young man, but until it is so presented he must fast\nand continue his purifications incessantly. It is a singular fact that nothing but\nthe spear of this armor is ever used in battle, though it is always carried when the\nowner accompanies a war party. At all times and under all circumstances the taboo or wohduze is\nupon it, until by slaying numerous enemies it is gradually removed. George Bushotter, a Teton. As he did not famish his description of
the dance in a single text, but in several, which were written on different occasions, it devolved on the present writer to undertake an
arrangement of the material after translating it. The accompanying
illustrations were made by Mr. Bushotter.

§ 144. Object of the sun dance. — ^The Dakota name for the sun dance
is ^'Wi wa"-yafig wa-tci-pi (Wi wai}yai}g wa6ipi), literally, ^* Sun fooking-at they-dance.'' The following are assigned Jis the reasons for cele-
brating this dance: During any winter when the people suffer from
famine or an epidemic, or when they wish to kill any enemy, or they
desire horses or an abundance of fruits and vegetables during the
coming summer, different Indians pray mentally to the sun, and each
one says, " Well, I will pray to Wakantanka early in the summer.^
Throughout the winter all those men who have made such vows take
frequent baths in sweat lodges. Each of these devotees or candidates
invites persons to a feast, on which occasion he joins his guests in
drinking great quantities of various kinds of herb teas. Then the
host notifies the guests of his vow, and from that time forward the
people treat him with great respect.

§145. Rvles observed by households. — The members of the households
of the devotees always abstain from loud talking and from bad acts of
various kinds. The following rules must be observed in the lodge of
each devotee : A piece of the soil is cut off between the back of the lodge
and the fireplace, and when virgin earth is reached vermilion is scattered over the exposed place. When the men smoke their pipes and
have burned out all of the tobacco in their pipe bowls, they must not
throw away the ashes as they would common refuse; they must be
carefal to empty the ashes on the exposed earth at the back of the
lodge. No one ventures to step on that virgin earth, and not even a
hand is ever stretched toward it. Only the man who expects to participate in the sun-dance can empty the ashes there, and after so doing
he returns each pii)e to its owner.

$ 146. The *' V-ma-neJ^—^^ The meUowed earth space, U-ma-ne
in Dakota, aud called by some peculiar names in other tribes,
has never been absent from any religions exercise I have yet

seen or learned of from the Indians. It represents the uuap- ■ ■ ''\

propriated life or power of the earth, hence man may obtain
it. The square or oblong, with the four lines standing out, is
invariably interpreted to mean the earth or laud with the four
winds st-andiug toward it. The cross, whether diagonal or upright, always symbolizes the four winds or four quarters." ' ^'®- 18»— The^jU mane"

Miss Fletcher uses this term, " U-ma-ne,'' to denote two things: the mellowed earth space (probably answering to the
u-j6-:^i of the Omaha and Ponka) and the symbol of the earth and the
four winds made within that mellowed earth space. A sketch of the
latter symbol is shown in Fig. 189. (See §§ 112, 155, etc. ; also Contr.
N. A. Ethn., Vol. vi,— 471-475.)

> Mias Fletcher, hi Rept. Peabody Maaeain, vol. lu, p. 284, note.

§ 147. Rules observed by the devotee. — Duriug the time of preparation
the devotee goes hunting, and if he kills a deer or buffalo he cuts up
the body in a '* wakan" manner. He skins it, but leaves the horns attached to the skull. He reddens the skin all over, and in the rear of
the lodge, in the open air, he prepares a bed of wild sage {Artetnisia)^
on which he lays the skull. He erects a post, on which he hangs a
tobacco pouch and a robe that is to be offered as a sacrifice. When
the devotee takes a meal everything which he touches must be perfectly
clean. He uses a new knife, which no one else dares to handle. Whatever he eats must be prepared in the best possible manner by the other
members of the household. They make for him a new pipe ornamented
with porcupine work, a new tobacco pouch, and a stick for pushing the
tobacco down into the bowl, both ornamented in like manner.

§ 148. The devotee must not go swimming, but he can enter the sweatlodge. There he rubs his body all over with wild sage; he cannot use
calico or cotton for that purpose. No unclean person of either sex
must go near him. The devotee is prohibited from fighting, even
should the camp be attacked. He must not act hastily, but at all times
must he proceed leisurely. He has his regular periods for crying and
praying.*

§149. All his female kindred make many pairs of moccasins and collect money and an abundance of all kinds of goods, in order to give
presents to poor people at the time of the sun dance. Then they can
make gifts to whomsoever they please, and on that account they will
win the right to have a child's ears pierced. The goods or horses,
ou account of which the child's ears are to be pierced, are reserved
for that occasion at some other place. The man whose office it will,
be to pierce the children's ears has to be notified in advance that
his services will be required. (See §206.)

. TRIBE.S INVITED TO THE 8UN-DANCB.

/ ^^ •

§ 160. When the devotees have performed all the preliminary duties
required of them, messages are sent to all the neighboring tribes,
i. e.j the Omaha, Pawnee Loup, Cheyenne, Eee, Hidatsa, Blackfeet,
J^ez Perc6, Winnebago, Yankton, and Santee. The latter part of
June is fixed upon as the time for the dance. (See §§ 138, 141.) The
visitors from the different nations begin to come together in the spring,
each visiting tribe forming its separate camp. Though some of the
visitors are hereditary enemies, it matters not during the sun-dance;
they visit one another; they shake hands and form alliances. In this
manner several weeks are spent very pleasantly."

tribe. As many men as are able to participate in that dance march
